problem.paragraph: 5. Details Two curves and their tangent lines intersecting at (2, 0) are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve f enters the fourth quadrant, goes up and to the right, concave down, crosses the x axis at (2, 0), and exits the viewing window in the first quadrant at the top right. Its tangent line labeled y = 1.8(x minus 2) enters the fourth quadrant to the left of curve f, goes up and to the right, touches the curve exactly once at (2, 0), and exits the viewing window in the first quadrant to the left of curve f. The curve g enters the fourth quadrant to the left of curve f, goes up and to the right, concave down, crosses the x axis at (2, 0), and exits the first quadrant below the curve f. Its tangent line labeled y = (4/5) times (x minus 2) enters the third quadrant to the left of curve g, goes up and to the right, touches the curve g at (2, 0), and exits the viewing window between the curves f and g. $$\frac{9}{4}$$

6. Details Two curves and their tangent lines intersecting at (2, 0) are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve labeled f enters the third quadrant, goes up and to the right through the fourth quadrant, concave up, crosses the x axis at (2, 0), then enters into the first quadrant, now concave down, and exits the viewing window at the right. The tangent line y = 1.5(x minus 2) with a positive slope enters the fourth quadrant to the right of curve f, goes up and to the right, touches the curve f exactly once at (2, 0), and exits the viewing window to the left of curve f. The curve labeled g enters the second quadrant, goes down and to the right through the first quadrant, concave down, crosses the x axis at (2, 0), and then extends into the fourth quadrant. The tangent line y = 2 minus x with a negative slope enters the second quadrant above the curve g, goes down and to the right through the first quadrant, touches the curve exactly once at (2, 0), and extends into the fourth quadrant above the curve g.
The graph of a function $$f$$ and its tangent line at $$0$$ are shown. What is the value of $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x)}{e^{ x} - 1}$$ ?

The line y = x is drawn from the third quadrant to the first quadrant through the origin, intersecting the curve near its low point in the third quadrant, and touching the curve at the origin.

exercises.paragraph: Source: Adapted from W. Stiles and B. Crawford, “The Luminous Efficiency of Rays Entering the Eye Pupil at Different Points.” Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, Series B: Biological Sciences 112 (1933): 428–50.

problem.paragraph: Investigate the family of curves $$f(x) = e^{ x} - cx$$ . In particular, find the limits as $$\left. x\rightarrow \pm \infty \right.$$ and determine the values of $$c$$ for which $$f$$ has an absolute minimum. What happens to the minimum points as $$c$$ increases?

solution.paragraph: $$f$$ has an absolute minimum for $$c > 0$$ . As $$c$$ increases, the minimum points get farther away from the origin.

Light enters the eye through the pupil and strikes the retina, where photoreceptor cells sense light and color. W. Stanley Stiles and B. H. Crawford studied the phenomenon in which measured brightness decreases as light enters farther from the center of the pupil (see the figure).

image.alt: Details An illustration shows an eye diagram and two light beams A and B striking the retina. A beam of light A runs horizontally through the center of the pupil and reaches the retina. Another beam of light B enters above light beam A, runs horizontally until it reaches near the edge of the pupil, a little away from the center of the pupil, then slants downward, and reaches the retina.

figure.caption: A light beam A that enters through the center of the pupil measures brighter than a beam B entering near the edge of the pupil.

problem.paragraph: They detailed their findings of this phenomenon, known as the Stiles–Crawford effect of the first kind, in an important paper published in 1933. In particular, they observed that the amount of luminance sensed was not proportional to the area of the pupil as they expected. The percentage $$P$$ of the total luminance entering a pupil of radius $$r$$ mm that is sensed at the retina can be described by
where $$\rho$$ is an experimentally determined constant, typically about $$0.05$$ .

list.item: What is the percentage of luminance sensed by a pupil of radius $$3$$ mm? Use $$\rho = 0.05$$ .
Compute the percentage of luminance sensed by a pupil of radius $$2$$ mm. Does it make sense that it is larger than the answer to part (a)?
Compute $$\lim\limits_{r\rightarrow 0^{+}}P$$ . Is the result what you would expect? Is this result physically possible?

The first appearance in print of l’Hospital’s Rule was in the book Analyse des infiniment petits published by the Marquis de l’Hospital in 1696. This was the first calculus textbook ever published. The example that the Marquis used in that book to illustrate his rule was to find the limit of the function
as $$x$$ approaches $$a$$ , where $$a > 0$$ . (At that time it was common to write $$aa$$ instead of $$a^{2}$$ .) Solve this problem.
